guide.title: How to use Mindkeep
guide.intro: Mindkeep is a workspace for the day — tasks, review, notes, habits, money, and nutrition. Right after you sign up, you choose which of these you want. The rest stay hidden until you turn them on.

steps.title: Create an account
steps.body: Sign up with email (a login code follows) or Google. Your timezone is detected automatically so task and review dates land on the right day.

steps.title: Choose what you use
steps.body: A short quiz asks which services you want, with a plain explanation of each. You can change this later in More → Settings. Anything you leave off does not appear in the menu or on the overview.

steps.title: Open the overview
steps.body: You see only the services you switched on. Empty blocks in the first days are normal.

steps.title: Plan the day
steps.body: Add a task with a title and how many minutes it takes. If it must not slip, tap Important: it appears in notifications at once so you are reminded in advance, and the calendar marks that day with a flag.

steps.title: Save what you learned
steps.body: After a lesson or practice, add a material. Mindkeep schedules reviews for day 3, 7, and 30.

steps.title: Log money movement
steps.body: In Budget, choose cash or card first, then the currency. Each currency stays on its own — no converted totals.

steps.title: Return via calendars
steps.body: Task and review calendars show what is due, what is late, and which days have important tasks.

rules: After registration you pick your services. Change them anytime in More → Settings.
Mark a task Important and it shows in the bell immediately — you do not wait for a later reminder.
The 3 / 7 / 30 review schedule is counted from the learning date and does not shift after completion.
Each operation has its own currency. Totals stay in that currency and are not converted.
Your data belongs only to your account and is not visible to other users.

faq.question: Where should I start?
faq.answer: After the quiz, open one of the services you picked: a task for today, a first review material, or an income/expense entry.

faq.question: Do I have to use every section?
faq.answer: No. The quiz is there so the cabinet stays uncluttered. Turn services on or off later in Settings.

faq.question: What does Important on a task do?
faq.answer: It flags the task as very important. A notification appears at once in the bell, and the task calendar marks that day, so you are reminded before it slips.

faq.question: What can I add as materials?
faq.answer: Words, notes, formulas, rules, work decisions, links — anything you want to revisit.

faq.question: Which currency is the budget in?
faq.answer: You choose the currency for each operation. Totals are not converted between currencies.

guide.ctaSubtitle: Add a task, a material, or a finance entry — and see how Mindkeep gathers the day in one place.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: This policy explains what data Mindkeep collects, why we need it, and how we protect it. By using the service, you agree to the practices described below.

sections.title: 1. Who is responsible
body: Mindkeep is operated by WEISEZAHOY studio.
For personal data requests, contact the email listed on this page.

sections.title: 2. What we collect
body: Account data: name, email, and a hashed password when you register.
Learning content: materials, categories, learned dates, and review statuses.
Technical data: timezone, interface language, and basic server logs needed for security and reliability.
If you use food scan on the mobile website, the photo is processed to estimate a meal name and calories and is not saved on our servers.

sections.title: 3. Why we use data
body: To create your account, store materials, and schedule reminders after 3, 7, and 30 days.
To show calendar, statistics, and in-app notifications.
To keep the service secure, prevent abuse, and improve reliability.

sections.title: 4. Storage and security
body: Data is stored on secured servers and transferred over HTTPS where available.
Passwords are never stored in plain text — we use cryptographic hashing.
Admin access is limited to authorized operators.

sections.title: 5. Sharing with third parties
body: We do not sell personal data.
Hosting and database providers may process data only to run Mindkeep under agreement with the operator.
If you subscribe, Stripe processes the payment and receives email and billing details needed to charge the card.
If you scan a meal on the mobile website, the photo is sent to Google Gemini only to estimate calories and is discarded afterwards. We do not store the photo.
If you photograph a receipt or bank statement in Budget, the photo is sent to Google Gemini only to read operations and is discarded afterwards. We do not store the photo.

sections.title: 6. Your rights
body: You can delete your account in Account on the website or in the app. That removes your notes, tasks, reviews, finance, and other personal data from our servers.
You can change language, theme, and learning content at any time inside the app.

sections.title: 7. Cookies and local data
body: Mindkeep may store a session token, language, and theme preference locally in your browser.
These are used for sign-in and interface comfort, not for advertising tracking.

sections.title: 8. Policy updates
body: We may update this policy. The current version is always available on this page with the update date.

blog.title: Review, focus, and what to keep
blog.subtitle: Three short notes: why 3·7·30, how Pomodoro helps you capture, and the 80/20 cut.

spaced-repetition.label: Spaced repetition
spaced-repetition.description: How timed revisits turn fragile memory into lasting recall.

pomodoro.label: Pomodoro
pomodoro.description: Short focused sprints that protect attention while you learn.

pareto.label: 80/20 results
pareto.description: Find the vital few inputs that move most of your progress.

spaced-repetition-memory.title: Why revisiting on day 3, 7 and 30 works
spaced-repetition-memory.excerpt: A calm guide to spaced repetition — and why Mindkeep keeps intervals fixed.
spaced-repetition-memory.originNote: Hermann Ebbinghaus mapped the forgetting curve in the 1880s. His work inspired spaced revisits that strengthen memory before it fades.
body: Learning is not a single moment — it is a series of returns. When you meet an idea once, the trace is fragile. When you meet it again at the right distance, the mind rebuilds the path with less effort and more clarity.

Spaced repetition grew from that insight: schedule reviews before forgetting wins. Classic systems adapt the gap after every answer. Mindkeep chooses a gentler contract — fixed revisits on day 3, day 7 and day 30 from the day you learned something.
Fixed intervals remove the noise of scoring yourself. You still revisit on purpose. You still protect long-term memory. You simply trust a clear rhythm instead of an ever-shifting algorithm.
Use this template whenever you write about memory: start with the feeling of forgetting, name the method, credit the originator, then connect it to how Mindkeep behaves in practice.

pomodoro-focus.title: Pomodoro: learn in bright, short windows
pomodoro-focus.excerpt: How 25-minute focus blocks help you study without burning out.
pomodoro-focus.originNote: Francesco Cirillo created the Pomodoro Technique in the late 1980s, naming it after a tomato-shaped kitchen timer.
body: Deep learning needs attention — and attention loves edges. A short, protected block tells your mind: this window is for one thing only.

The Pomodoro pattern is simple: focus for about 25 minutes, then rest briefly. After a few cycles, take a longer pause. The point is not perfection. The point is a repeatable cadence that keeps energy available for the next return.
Pair Pomodoro with Mindkeep: use a focus block to capture what you learned, then let the 3 · 7 · 30 schedule bring you back later. Capture now. Revisit later. Protect both intensity and memory.
When you draft future articles on focus, keep this shape: problem of distraction → Cirillo’s method → practical pairing with Mindkeep → one gentle invitation to try today.

pareto-learning-results.title: The 80/20 rule in learning
pareto-learning-results.excerpt: How Vilfredo Pareto’s insight helps you choose what is worth remembering.
pareto-learning-results.originNote: Economist Vilfredo Pareto observed that a minority of causes often drive a majority of outcomes — later popularized as the 80/20 principle.
body: Not every fact deserves the same space in your mind. Some ideas unlock many others. Some only decorate the surface.

The Pareto principle suggests a useful bias: look for the vital few. In language learning that may be high-frequency words. In coding it may be the patterns you reuse weekly. In work it may be the principles behind your best decisions.
Mindkeep helps you keep what you chose — not everything you touched. Capture the material that compounds. Review it on a fixed rhythm. Leave the rest outside the schedule so attention stays sharp.
Template for future 80/20 notes: name the overcrowded effort → introduce Pareto → give one concrete learning example → show how Mindkeep protects the vital few with 3 · 7 · 30 revisits.
